# Net PP&E, depreciation, capital expenditure

## Three lines {.plain-title}

$$\text{Net PP\&E}_t = k \times \text{Sales}_{t+1}$$

$$\text{Depreciation}_t = d \times \text{Net PP\&E}_{t-1}$$

$$\text{CapEx}_t = \text{Net PP\&E}_t - \text{Net PP\&E}_{t-1} + \text{Depreciation}_t$$

Net PP&E and the depreciation rate are assumptions. Capital expenditure is
computed from them.

## Capital expenditure as the residual {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[The asset base is the assumption]{.card-title}

Capacity is in place before the sales it serves, so the balance at the end of
year $t$ carries year $t+1$'s sales.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Depreciation follows the balance]{.card-title}

A percentage of the opening net balance, not a percentage of sales.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Capital expenditure is the residual]{.card-title}

It funds the increase in the balance and replaces what was depreciated during
the year.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[The zero-growth check]{.card-title}

If the balance never changes, capital expenditure equals depreciation.
:::
:::

# The project that does not end

## Drop the sale, keep the ratios {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[No sale]{.card-title}

The 19.59 of book value stays in the business.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Year 5 keeps investing]{.card-title}

Capital expenditure of 3.92 and another 0.35 of working capital, building for
year 6.
:::
:::

| $ millions | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Free cash flow | 3.52 | 3.80 | 4.11 | 4.43 | 4.79 |
| Share of sales | 11.0% | 11.0% | 11.0% | 11.0% | 11.0% |

## Every line is a multiple of sales {.plain-title}

Constant growth and constant ratios mean free cash flow grows at the sales rate
forever.

$$V_0 = \frac{\text{FCF}_1}{r-g} = \frac{3.52}{0.12-0.08} = 88.00$$

::: {.note}
Against 19.20 of capital at date 0, an NPV of 68.80 &mdash; against 11.44 when
the same business was sold at book in year 5.
:::

# Two-stage growth

## The first three years, and then 8% {.plain-title}

The same company, with sales that reach 8% only in year 4: 25% growth in year
2, 15% in year 3, and a margin that climbs to 25% over the same three years. It
holds 6.00 of cash and 18.00 of debt, against 4.0 million shares.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Years 1 to 3]{.card-title}

Sales grow 25% and then 15%. The EBITDA margin climbs from 18% to 21% to 23%.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Year 4 onward]{.card-title}

Sales grow 8% a year and the margin holds at 25%. The three ratios are fixed
throughout.
:::
:::

# Terminal value

## Free cash flow in year 5 {.plain-title}

Free cash flow reaches 11.0% of sales in year 4 and stays there: the margin and
all three ratios are fixed from year 4 on. Sales grow 8% in year 5 and every
year after, so free cash flow does too.

::: {.note}
Year 4 is the first year at the steady ratio. Year 5 is the first year that
grows at 8%, which is why the terminal value sits at the end of year 4.
:::

## The terminal value {.plain-title}

$$\text{TV}_4 = \frac{\text{FCF}_5}{r-g} = \frac{5.90}{0.12-0.08} = 147.55$$

::: {.note}
Twenty-five times year-5 free cash flow, at a four-point spread between $r$ and
$g$.
:::

## Discount it all back {.plain-title}

| $ millions | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | TV at 4, year 5 on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Cash flow | (1.51) | 1.46 | 4.33 | 5.46 | 147.55 |
| Discount factor at 12% | 0.893 | 0.797 | 0.712 | 0.636 | 0.636 |
| Present value | (1.35) | 1.16 | 3.08 | 3.47 | 93.77 |

::: {.stats}
::: {.stat}
[$100.14m]{.stat-value}
[Enterprise value]{.stat-label}
:::

::: {.stat}
[94%]{.stat-value}
[In the terminal value]{.stat-label}
:::
:::

## Where the 8% comes from {.plain-title}

$$g = \text{ROIC} \times \text{reinvestment rate}$$

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[ROIC]{.card-title}

$8.48 / 32.20 = 26.3\%$
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Reinvestment rate]{.card-title}

$(4.83 + 0.43 - 2.68) / 8.48 = 30.4\%$
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Product]{.card-title}

$26.3\% \times 30.4\% = 8.0\%$
:::
:::

Year-5 figures, against net PP&E plus working capital of 32.20 at the end of
year 4.

# Cash and debt

## From enterprise value to equity {.plain-title}

| $ millions | |
|---|---:|
| Enterprise value | 100.14 |
| Plus cash | 6.00 |
| Less debt | (18.00) |
| Equity value | 88.14 |

## Two points about the equity value calculation {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Cash is not working capital]{.card-title}

The 10% ratio covers receivables, inventory and payables. Cash is added
separately, at face value.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Interest is not in free cash flow]{.card-title}

The cash flows are unlevered. Debt enters through the WACC and again in the
equity value calculation, never in the forecast.
:::
:::

# John B. Sanfilippo & Son

## The company {.plain-title}

Shells, roasts and packages nuts. Fisher, Orchard Valley Harvest, Squirrel
Brand, and private label for the grocery chains. Fiscal years end in late June.

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Ticker]{.card-title}

`JBSS`, $805 million of market value: 11.78 million diluted shares at $68.31.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[What it owns]{.card-title}

Shelling and roasting plants, $268 million of net PP&E against $1.18 billion
of sales.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[The balance sheet]{.card-title}

Simple. The company owns no other businesses, and goodwill is $11.8 million
against $659 million of assets.
:::
:::

## Four years of history {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| $ millions | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sales | 999.7 | 1,066.8 | 1,107.2 | 1,175.7 |
| Sales growth | &mdash; | 6.7% | 3.8% | 6.2% |
| Operating income | 88.9 | 81.7 | 82.9 | 87.0 |
| Operating margin | 8.9% | 7.7% | 7.5% | 7.4% |
| Net PP&E | 127.2 | 178.6 | 193.0 | 268.3 |
| Depreciation | 22.1 | 26.6 | 31.5 | 33.3 |
| Capital expenditure | 20.7 | 28.3 | 50.7 | 88.1 |

::: {.note}
Yahoo returns four years for JBSS, not five, and each ratio needs three.
:::

## The three ratios, measured {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Net PP&E / next year's sales ($k$) | 11.9% | 16.1% | 16.4% | &mdash; |
| Depreciation / opening net PP&E ($d$) | &mdash; | 20.9% | 17.6% | 17.3% |
| Working capital / next year's sales ($w$) | 15.7% | 17.1% | 21.1% | &mdash; |

$k$ and $w$ are measured against next year's sales, so they stop at FY2025, the
last year with a following year in the data.

## Capital expenditure and net PP&E {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Three years above depreciation]{.card-title}

Capital expenditure of 28.3, 50.7, 88.1 against depreciation of 26.6, 31.5,
33.3. FY2023 was the last year capital expenditure ran below depreciation.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[So net PP&E doubles]{.card-title}

Net PP&E goes from 127.2 to 268.3 while sales rise 18%. The FY2024 step is a
$59.0m acquisition, almost all of it plant. The FY2026 step is the build.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[So $k$ doubles]{.card-title}

$k$ goes from 11.9% to 16.4%, and is 21.6% measured against the FY2027 sales
forecast.
:::
:::

The forecast has to say whether net PP&E stays this high relative to sales.

## The other two ratios {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[$d$ falls for a mechanical reason]{.card-title}

$d$ goes from 20.9% to 17.3%. New assets enter net PP&E faster than the existing
assets are depreciated, so $d$ falls even though the depreciable lives have not
changed. Of the 268.3 balance, 86.9 is construction in progress, which does not
depreciate until it is in service. Call $d$ 15%.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[$w$ moves with inventory]{.card-title}

$w$ goes from 15.7% to 21.1%. Inventory alone is 245.8 against net working
capital of 220.1, and a nut processor buys a crop once a year. Call $w$ 18%.
:::
:::

# Accounting

## Leases: finance or operating {.plain-title}

Does the lease hand over substantially all the risks and rewards of owning the
asset? If so it is a purchase the lessor financed. Any one of five tests settles
it.

::: {.steps}
1. Ownership transfers at the end of the term
2. There is a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to take
3. The term covers a major part of the asset's remaining economic life
4. The payments are worth substantially all of the asset's fair value
5. The asset is so specialised it has no other use to the lessor
:::

Meet none of the five and it is an operating lease.

## Leases: what the choice is {.plain-title}

Both sit on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. A
finance lease splits into depreciation and interest; an operating lease is rent
in EBIT.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Leave the rent in EBIT]{.card-title}

The right-of-use asset stays out of invested capital and the lease liability out
of the equity value calculation. The rent is already subtracted in EBIT.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Or capitalise the lease]{.card-title}

Take the rent out of EBIT and depreciate the right-of-use asset in its place.
The asset joins invested capital and the lease liability joins the equity value
calculation.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
Either is defensible. Half of the second &mdash; the lease liability subtracted
in the equity value calculation, the rent still in EBIT &mdash; charges twice.
:::

## Leases: read the debt line twice {.plain-title}

Yahoo reports total debt of 104.1. That is not what the company borrowed.

| $ millions | |
|---|---:|
| Long-term debt | 43.6 |
| Current debt | 39.9 |
| Borrowings | 83.5 |
| Operating lease liability, non-current | 20.6 |
| Yahoo's "total debt" | 104.1 |

::: {.note}
No finance leases. The rent is still inside the 87.0 of operating income, so the
20.6 is not subtracted when computing equity value. Subtracting it anyway lowers
the value by $1.75 a share.
:::

## Deferred taxes: check, then ignore {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Book effective rate | 24.6% | 24.3% | 25.4% |
| Cash taxes paid / pretax income | 27.7% | 27.2% | 16.7% |

Cash taxes ran 23.8% over the three years against a book rate of 24.8%. Taxing
EBIT at the cash rate instead would add about $1.64 a share.

::: {.note}
A one-point gap is small enough to leave the forecast taxing EBIT at the book
rate.
:::

## Goodwill, intangibles, and other liabilities {.plain-title}

::: {.cards .cards-3}
::: {.card}
[Goodwill, $11.8m]{.card-title}

1.8% of assets. No acquisitions are forecast, so goodwill is held flat and added
in the equity value calculation, where it adds a dollar a share.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Other intangibles, $3.4m]{.card-title}

Held flat and added in the equity value calculation too, where they add 29 cents
a share.
:::

::: {.card .card-sand}
[Other long-term liabilities, $6.6m]{.card-title}

The whole "other" category on the balance sheet, and the only one of these three
items subtracted in the equity value calculation rather than added.
:::
:::

The three items together move the value per share by 73 cents, against a $5.30
gap to the market price.

## One rule {.plain-title}

Every balance sheet item goes in exactly one of two places.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[Invested capital]{.card-title}

An item goes here if it produces the operating cash flows being discounted. The
change in the item is a cash flow in the forecast.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[The equity value calculation]{.card-title}

Every other item goes here, carried at book value between enterprise value and
equity value.
:::
:::

::: {.note}
Putting an item in both double counts it; leaving it out of both drops it from
the valuation.
:::

## Sensitivity to $k$ {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| | Value per share |
|---|---:|
| $k$ back to 16.4%, the recent plant spending was a one-off | $80.73 |
| $k$ at 21.0%, the base case | $73.61 |
| $k$ at 21.6%, today's level holds | $72.68 |

::: {.note}
$d$ does not appear in this table, and cannot. Capital expenditure less
depreciation is the change in the net PP&E balance, and EBIT here is a margin
on sales rather than EBITDA less depreciation. So $d$ cancels out of the
valuation.
:::

# If there is time

## Smith-Midland {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

Precast concrete: highway barriers, sound walls, building panels. `SMID`, $130
million of market value at $24.54 a share.

| $ millions | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sales | 50.1 | 59.6 | 78.5 | 93.4 |
| Sales growth | &mdash; | 18.8% | 31.8% | 19.0% |
| Operating margin | 1.7% | 1.9% | 12.6% | 18.2% |
| Net PP&E | 25.1 | 27.7 | 31.7 | 38.5 |
| Depreciation | 2.9 | 2.4 | 2.7 | 2.9 |
| Capital expenditure | 2.7 | 5.0 | 6.2 | 9.3 |

## The three ratios, measured {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $k$ | 42.2% | 35.3% | 33.9% | &mdash; |
| $d$ | &mdash; | 9.5% | 9.6% | 9.1% |
| $w$ | 19.6% | 11.2% | 14.9% | &mdash; |

::: {.note}
$k$ in the mid-thirties is nearly twice JBSS's $k$: a concrete plant carries
just under three dollars of sales per dollar of net PP&E. $d$ holds between
9.1% and 9.6%. The operating margin is the line that moves, from 1.7% to 18.2%.
:::

## The forecast {.plain-title}

| Item | Assumption |
|---|---|
| Sales growth | 12%, 9%, 6%, then 3% |
| Operating margin | 13.0%, down from 18.2% |
| Net PP&E ($k$) | 36.0% of next year's sales |
| Depreciation ($d$) | 9.5% of opening net PP&E |
| Working capital ($w$) | 18.0% of next year's sales |
| Tax rate, WACC | 25%, 11% |

Everything but the operating margin is read off the history.

## The schedule and the cash flow {.plain-title .nowrap-labels}

| $ millions | FY25 | FY26 | FY27 | FY28 | FY29 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sales | 93.4 | 104.6 | 114.0 | 120.9 | 124.5 |
| Net PP&E | 38.5 | 41.0 | 43.5 | 44.8 | 46.2 |
| Depreciation | &mdash; | 3.7 | 3.9 | 4.1 | 4.3 |
| Capital expenditure | &mdash; | 6.2 | 6.4 | 5.4 | 5.6 |
| Working capital | 23.2 | 20.5 | 21.8 | 22.4 | 23.1 |
| Free cash flow | &mdash; | 10.3 | 7.4 | 9.8 | 10.1 |

::: {.note}
FY2026 working capital falls because the assumed $w$ of 18% is below the 22.2%
the company carried at FY2025. A ratio assumption applied to an actual balance
always steps in year one.
:::

## The value {.plain-title}

$$\text{TV}_{2029} = \frac{10.1 \times 1.03}{0.11-0.03} = 130.3$$

| $ millions | |
|---|---:|
| Present value of FY26 to FY29 | 29.2 |
| Present value of terminal value | 85.8 |
| Enterprise value | 115.0 |
| Plus cash, less debt | 11.9, (4.5) |
| Equity value | 122.4 |
| Value per share, on 5.31m shares | $23.05 |

# Assignment

## Flexsteel {.plain-title}

Value Flexsteel the way we valued JBSS. Yahoo Finance, ticker `FLXS`, fiscal
years ending June 30.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[What it does]{.card-title}

Makes and sells upholstered furniture. Four years of data, FY2023 through
FY2026.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[Why this one]{.card-title}

All three ratios move over the four years, so each one has to be defended rather
than read off the history.
:::
:::

## What to pull {.plain-title}

| Statement | Lines |
|---|---|
| Income statement | Revenue, operating income, pretax income, tax provision, diluted shares |
| Balance sheet | Cash, current assets, current liabilities, current debt, net PP&E, total debt, operating lease liability |
| Cash flow | Depreciation and amortisation, capital expenditure |

Net working capital is current assets less cash, minus current liabilities less
current debt.

## Part 1: the three ratios {.plain-title}

Compute, for every year the data allows:

::: {.steps}
1. $k$, net PP&E as a share of next year's sales
2. $d$, depreciation as a share of opening net PP&E
3. $w$, net working capital as a share of next year's sales
:::

Report each ratio year by year. Two of the three fall by about a third over the
four years and the third rises. Say what single fact about the company explains
all three, and whether that change is finished.

## Part 2: the forecast {.plain-title}

| Item | Assumption |
|---|---|
| Sales growth | 5.0%, 4.5%, 4.0%, then 3.0% |
| Operating margin | 8.5%, held |
| Net PP&E ($k$) | 16.0% of next year's sales |
| Depreciation ($d$) | 5.0% of opening net PP&E |
| Working capital ($w$) | 16.0% of next year's sales |
| Tax rate | 25% |
| WACC | 10.5% |

Use these, not your own averages, so the answers are comparable.

## Part 3: the value {.plain-title}

::: {.steps}
1. The capital schedule and free cash flow for FY2027 to FY2030
2. Terminal value at the end of FY2030, and the enterprise value
3. Equity value per share, and the comparison to the market price
:::

| For the equity value calculation, at FY2026 | $ millions |
|---|---:|
| Borrowings | 0.0 |
| Operating lease liability | 51.9 |
| Cash | 16.7 |
| Share price | $82.11 |

The share count is not in the table. Part 4 asks for it.

## Part 4: the accounting {.plain-title}

Answer in a sentence each.

::: {.cards .cards-2}
::: {.card}
[The depreciable life]{.card-title}

Your $d$ will come out near 4%, an implied life above twenty years for a
furniture maker's plant. Explain the long implied life, and name the balance
sheet line that is the evidence.
:::

::: {.card .card-blue}
[The debt line]{.card-title}

Yahoo reports total debt of 51.9 and the company has no borrowings. Say what the
51.9 is, whether it belongs in your equity value calculation, and what you would
have to change in the forecast to put it there.
:::
:::

Diluted average shares for FY2026 are 5.46 million. Shares outstanding on the
cover of the 10-K are 4.11 million. Say which one belongs in the equity value

:::
